title: Network hardening and terraform adapter guidance (draft)
body:
Purpose and scope:

This doc is a working draft describing a minimal, audit-friendly path to harden customer VPC/network attachments for private deployments (VPC peering, interconnects, and on-prem cross-connects). It focuses on an "adapter"-style Terraform approach that lets us incrementally introduce stricter controls (egress filtering, IP allowlists, host isolation) without full greenfield rewrites or long maintenance windows.

Audience:
- Solutions engineers and infra SREs running customer on-prem / VPC installs
- Terraform module maintainers who implement network adapters
- Security reviewers and compliance engineers

High-level goals (non-exhaustive):
1) Provide a repeatable migration pattern that can be applied per-customer with minimal traffic disruption.
2) Centralize policy in reusable TF modules (adapter pattern) so rollbacks and tweaks are simple.
3) Ensure all changes are auditable with clear test gates and fallback plans.
4) Protect customer data paths via egress filtering and optional per-tenant NAT.

Why an "adapter" module?
- Many customers arrive with diverse network topologies. A single big-bang module rarely fits.
- Adapter module = a thin shim that maps our canonical security model onto customer networking primitives (cloud routers, transit, firewalls).
- This lets infra teams swap or upgrade the canonical implementation behind a stable interface.

Canonical requirements for adapter interface (module-level):
- Inputs: customer_vpc_cidr, mgmt_subnets, allowed_egress_ranges, onprem_cidrs, nat_mode (shared|per-tenant), enable_egress_filtering (bool), audit_log_bucket, maintenance_window (string)
- Outputs: adapter_id, effective_routes, egress_policy_version, tf_resource_map (list of resource addresses)
- Behavior: non-destructive by default (create-new-resources, do not replace customer-managed gateways unless explicit flag).

Core patterns to implement in adapter module (order matters):
1) Non-destructive overlay: create new transit/edge components and attach them in parallel, route gradually via BGP/route-priority.
2) Egress isolation modes:
   - permissive: allow all egress through customer-managed NAT (default for early phases)
   - filtered-shared-nat: shared NAT gateway with prefix-based egress ACLs
   - per-tenant-nat: tenant-dedicated NAT instances + per-tenant iptables/eBPF filter (strongest isolation)
3) Audit-first changes: enable flow logs/IAM logs to bucket before toggling policies.
4) Canary rollout: shift 5-10% of traffic via route-weights or policy-based routing, monitor logs for blocked flows.

Terraform notes and pitfalls:
- Keep state separation: adapter module should write to its own state file (or dedicated workspace) to avoid accidental replacement of customer-created resources.
- resource addresses in outputs: provide a stable mapping (module outputs that list resource addresses) for SRE to inspect and script rollbacks.
- Avoid lifecycle "create_before_destroy" where it touches customer-run gateways; instead, prefer "prevent_destroy" until explicit opt-in.
- Use data sources for existing resources (e.g., google_compute_router) and do not attempt to import them in the module automatically. Instead, expose an import_guidance output with CLI snippets.

Sample pseudo-Terraform interface (trimmed for doc):

module "network_adapter" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules//network-adapter?ref=staging"

  customer_vpc_cidr      = var.customer_vpc_cidr
  mgmt_subnets           = var.mgmt_subnets
  allowed_egress_ranges  = var.allowed_egress_ranges
  onprem_cidrs           = var.onprem_cidrs
  nat_mode               = var.nat_mode             # shared | per-tenant
  enable_egress_filtering= var.enable_egress_filtering
  audit_log_bucket       = var.audit_log_bucket
  maintenance_window     = var.maintenance_window
}

Notes on variables: keep defaults permissive. Early customers should not have connectivity broken by default. Set enable_egress_filtering=false in initial onboarding.

Migration plan (phased):
Phase 0 – Discovery and safe defaults (1–3 days)
- Inventory: run network scan (Nmap internally), collect route tables, BGP peers, firewall rules.
- Create adapter in permissive mode (enable_egress_filtering=false, nat_mode=shared).
- Turn on flow logging to S3/GCS and retention to 90 days.
- Smoke tests: ping from inside workload subnets to a staging endpoint, verify metrics.

Phase 1 – Observability and small hardening (week 1)
- Enable per-subnet flow log tags.
- Introduce ACLs for management subnets (deny all but SSH/HTTPS from operator IP ranges).
- Run a 2-hour canary: shift a small route prefix to the adapter and validate allowed services.
- Review blocked flow logs and document false positives in audit ticket.

Phase 2 – Controlled egress filtering (week 2–3)
- Set enable_egress_filtering=true, but keep nat_mode=shared.
- Deploy ACLs that only allow known egress ranges for model downloads, metrics endpoints, and telemetry.
- Maintain an "egress-exceptions" list; changes require PR + SOC review.

Phase 3 – Per-tenant isolation (optional, month 1)
- For customers needing strict separation, migrate to nat_mode=per-tenant.
- Migration steps: create per-tenant NAT devices in parallel, BGP advertise / allocate ephemeral prefixes, shift tenant prefixes one-by-one.
- Validation: separate metrics, flow logs partitioned by tenant. Rollback by reverting BGP advertisement.

Rollback and emergency plan:
- Every adapter change must expose a single toggle: adapter_force_pass_through = true. When set, adapter detaches filters and resumes permissive routing.
- If BGP reconfiguration fails, withdraw new advertisements and re-establish previous AS-paths. Document the exact "bgp withdraw" commands in the runbook.

Testing checklist (automated + manual):
- Unit: terraform plan does not propose changes to customer-managed routers by default.
- Integration: end-to-end connectivity tests to production-like staging endpoints.
- Security: run internal port-scan and verify ACLs block expected ports.
- Observability: confirm flow logs contain expected tags and are readable by downstream analytics.

Operational runbook snippets (commands):
- Export an adapter's resource map: terraform output -json tf_resource_map > adapter-map.json
- Force pass-through (emergency): terraform apply -var 'adapter_force_pass_through=true'
- Re-import an existing router (manual guidance output by module): gcloud compute routers import --source router-id --project X (see import_guidance output)

Audit and compliance notes:
- All changes that tighten egress must be accompanied by a documented risk assessment and approval from security (ticket in JIRA-SEC).
- Maintain a change log within the adapter module S3/GCS state metadata. We add commit hash + PR ref to every apply via a small wrapper script.

Edge cases and known tough customers:
- Carrier NAT customers: public IP exhaustion requires a special flow — we prefer per-tenant ephemeral prefix allocations instead of relying on shared public NAT.
- Air-gapped deployments: adapter will not create internet-facing NAT; instead, we recommend an upstream controlled egress proxy. Provide a minimal offline audit checklist.

Open technical questions (to resolve before wide rollout):
- Do we need a formal schema for egress-exceptions (JSON schema) or will a set of tag-based allowlists suffice?
- What is the expected RTO for per-tenant NAT migrations? (target: <30m, needs validation)
- How to handle multi-cloud customers that have overlapping CIDRs? Suggestion: require customer CIDR normalization step and provide an annotated map.

Next actions (owners and rough ETA):
- Marco: prototype adapter outputs with tf_resource_map + import_guidance (ETA: 2024-10-01)
- Sanya: create compliance checklist and JIRA template for egress changes (ETA: 2024-10-15)
- Tom: build small canary harness that can shift 10% traffic via route-weight (ETA: 2024-10-08)

Appendix A — Minimal test matrix (example)
- Test case: management console access after ACLs applied
  - Steps: apply ACL deny-all, add rule for operator IPs, attempt console access
  - Expected: operator can access; others cannot
- Test case: model download from S3 after egress filters
  - Steps: allow s3 ranges, attempt download from a worker node
  - Expected: download succeeds; blocked flows appear in logs with tag 'model-download'

Appendix B — Example change PR checklist
- Title: network-adapter: enable_egress_filtering=true for customer-XYZ
- Included: terraform plan output, flow-log sample, risk assessment doc link, rollback steps, maintenance window, approver from security

Appendix C — Quick troubleshooting notes
- If hosts report DNS failures after introducing filtering: verify UDP 53 is allowed to customer DNS forwarders and that DNAT rules are not accidentally applied to 53 only for TCP.
- If large numbers of blocked flows show up for telemetry endpoints: check TLS SNI differences (some SDKs use different hostnames) and add temporary egress-exception entries.

This doc is intentionally pragmatic and will be iterated. Please add comments inline or push small edits to the terraform-modules repo with references to this doc.
